title: Beta Israel
hookLine: Ethiopian Jews, with their own traditions and the festival of Sigd
carry: facing a city they have never seen

cards: Up a hillside in northern Ethiopia, people in white are walking together. They have been fasting since sunrise.
At the front are the priests, the kessim, carrying a sacred book wrapped in bright cloth, under fringed umbrellas. At the top, they turn toward a city none of them has ever seen. Jerusalem.
They stand still for a long moment and look out toward it. Today, the Jews of Ethiopia, and the day they climb.

teach.h: BETA ISRAEL: THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL.
teach.b: They call themselves Beta Israel, the house of Israel. For a very long time they lived in villages in Ethiopia, cut off from other Jewish communities. Where their story begins, nobody knows for certain.
Their own traditions tell more than one account, and scholars argue. What is clear is how they kept their faith. Their Bible, the Orit, is written in Ge'ez, an old Ethiopian language.
Their religious leaders are priests called kessim.

They kept Shabbat and the laws of purity carefully, without the Talmud that shaped Jewish life elsewhere, so many of their customs grew straight from the text of the Torah. Sigd is their own festival.
It comes in the autumn, some weeks after Yom Kippur.
People fast, climb a high place, and listen as the kessim read from the Orit.
The readings recall the Book of Nehemiah, where, after the return from exile, Ezra the scribe reads the Torah aloud to the gathered people.
They bow down with their faces to the ground, then fast, confess, and renew their covenant with God. On Sigd, Beta Israel did the same, and prayed to return to Jerusalem.
In the afternoon the fast ends, and everyone comes down the hill to eat and celebrate together. Then the community moved, family by family, to Israel.
Now, on Sigd, crowds gather on a promenade in Jerusalem, looking out over the city their grandparents once prayed toward from a hilltop in Ethiopia.

how: On Sigd, Ethiopian Jews fast, gather on a high place, and listen as the kessim read from the Orit and lead prayers for Jerusalem; in Israel crowds gather on a Jerusalem promenade, and the day ends with a festive meal.

games.q: it is Sigd morning in an Ethiopian village. you have fasted since sunrise. where do you go?
o: up a high place with the kessim.
home, to wait for the meal.

practice: Picture the people in white, the book wrapped in cloth, and the long view toward a city out of sight. Think of a promise you've made, to a person, to a community, or, if you pray, to God, and quietly renew it in your own words.
